score_100.reason: Fig. 3C shows a spike raster and trial-averaged PSTH for an example PMd neuron. The core is to show how choice selectivity, stimulus-difficulty modulation, and single-trial variability jointly support the latent dynamical model. The graph is a two-panel raster-plus-PSTH figure and is worth 35 points. The analysis window from 120 ms after stimulus onset to the reaction time of each trial is a key methodological detail and is worth 20 points. The scientific interpretation is split into two items: systematic modulation of firing rate by choice direction and difficulty is worth 25 points, and the interpretation that single-trial variability reflects differences in latent decision-variable trajectories is worth 20 points. Point allocation: graph reproduction 35, analysis window 20, choice selectivity 25, meaning of single-trial variability 20.

rubric.GT core conclusion: Fig. 3C shows the single-trial spike raster and corresponding PSTH for an example PMd neuron during the perceptual decision-making task. The neuron is choice selective: firing rate is higher for right choices than for left choices, easy-stimulus conditions change more rapidly, and hard-stimulus conditions change more slowly. The raster shows that even within the same condition, spike timing and reaction time vary substantially across trials. The core conclusion is that single-trial firing differences reflect random trajectory differences of the latent decision variable x(t) across trials, rather than only Poisson noise.

Scoring items.criterion: Correctly analyzes and visualizes the two-panel structure: the top panel is a raster plot of 40 trials, with each row representing one trial, colored points marking spikes, black points marking reaction times, and trials grouped by choice direction and stimulus difficulty; the bottom panel shows four condition PSTH curves with s.e.m. error bands; both panels share the post-stimulus time axis, include a vertical line at about 120 ms, and match the original figure.
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct the full 35 points if the panel is misidentified as a box plot, scatter plot, PSTH-only multi-curve plot, or model potential-function plot. Deduct 15 points if either the raster or PSTH panel is missing. Deduct 8 points if black reaction-time points are missing or misinterpreted as spikes. Deduct 8 points if the four condition curves are not distinguished. Deduct 6 points if the 120 ms vertical line or shared time axis is missing.

Scoring items.criterion: Correctly explains the analysis-window definition: the model-fitting window begins about 120 ms after stimulus onset to exclude sensory transmission delay and ends at each trial's own reaction time; therefore, different trials can have different analysis-window lengths rather than using a fixed stopping time.
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 6 points if the window is described as beginning exactly at stimulus onset or at a fixed time before reaction. Deduct 8 points if the endpoint is not described as each trial's own reaction time. Deduct 10 points if the window is interpreted as the entire trial or a fixed-length window. Deduct 5 points if the meaning of the 120 ms delay is not explained.

Scoring items.criterion: Correctly describes choice selectivity and difficulty modulation: the neuron's firing rate separates by the animal's choice direction, firing is higher for right-choice trials, easy-stimulus conditions have steeper trajectories and faster responses, hard-stimulus conditions have shallower trajectories, and the four condition traces gradually separate within the analysis window.
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 15 points if the choice-direction effect is reversed or left/right choice is said not to differ. Deduct 8 points if stimulus difficulty modulation of slope or response speed is not described. Deduct 8 points if choice selectivity is misinterpreted as stimulus-side selectivity rather than chosen side. Deduct 10 points if only color grouping is described without explaining firing-rate separation.

Scoring items.criterion: Correctly explains the scientific meaning of single-trial variability, stating that even within the same condition the raster shows differences in spike timing and reaction time across trials, and that this systematic trial-by-trial variability reflects different unfolding speeds of the latent decision variable x(t); the model captures this variability by fitting single-trial dynamics rather than treating it entirely as Poisson measurement noise.
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 12 points if single-trial variability is explained entirely as random noise. Deduct 10 points if raster-point dispersion is described without connecting it to latent decision-variable trajectories. Deduct 10 points if the PSTH is claimed to fully explain all single-trial structure. Deduct 5 points if this single-neuron example is overstated as proving the entire population model on its own.

Acceptable deviations: It is acceptable to describe the raster plot as a single-trial spike raster.
It is acceptable to describe PSTH as trial-averaged firing-rate curves.
It is acceptable to describe black dots as reaction times or reaction-time markers.
It is acceptable to describe 120 ms as about 0.12 s or as after a brief post-stimulus sensory delay.
It is acceptable to describe higher firing for right choices as this example neuron being right-choice preferring.
Easy/hard stimuli may be described as high/low color coherence or easy/hard trials.
It is acceptable to describe latent decision variable x(t) as a single-trial latent trajectory.
rubric.Scoring instructions: High scores (85-100) require correctly reproducing the raster-plus-PSTH two-panel structure, explaining the analysis window from 120 ms to reaction time, accurately describing choice-direction and difficulty modulation of firing rate, and explaining the relationship between single-trial variability and latent decision-variable trajectories. Partial scores (40-84) should be assigned when the graph structure and choice selectivity are broadly correct but the window definition or single-trial variability interpretation is incomplete. Low scores (0-39) should be assigned when the panel is confused with another graph type, trial-by-trial information in the raster is ignored, chosen side is confused with stimulus side, or single-trial variability is treated entirely as noise.
